title_en: The Three-Level Concentration of Tsinghua and Peking Seats: Where You Stand Beats How Hard You Try
excerpt_en: Six Haidian high schools send more students to Tsinghua and Peking University than most entire provinces. The seats were never really allocated by effort — they are allocated by location, three levels deep.
body_en:
Start with one number. In 2026, Beijing's six famous Haidian high schools — the High School Affiliated to Renmin University, the High School Affiliated to Tsinghua, the Affiliated High School of Peking University, Beijing National Day School, the High School Affiliated to Capital Normal University, and Beijing 101 Middle School — sent roughly 350 students to Tsinghua and Peking University combined.

What is 350? More than the total Tsinghua–Peking admissions of most entire provinces — in some provinces, several times more, even ten times more. Yet those six schools graduate only a few thousand students a year, while a single province fields several hundred thousand exam candidates.

Same exam, same papers. On one side the admission rate is measured in percent; on the other, in ten-thousandths. The difference is not effort. It is location.

Three levels of concentration: each layer eats the one below

Zoom out from Beijing to the provinces and the picture sharpens. Take Sichuan, a gaokao giant: the city of Chengdu alone accounts for about a third of the province's Tsinghua–Peking admissions. The schools that win those seats graduate only a few hundred students a year; Sichuan's candidate pool is over 500,000, among the five largest in China.

One six-hundredth of the people take a third of the seats. Spread across the map, the remaining two-thirds are divided among hundreds of counties and thousands of high schools — the other 499,400 candidates.

Sichuan is not special. Across the country, almost every city's Tsinghua–Peking admissions are concentrated in its best one to three schools. Only Beijing and Shanghai, drowning in educational resources, can spread them across four to eight.

The pattern compresses into three sentences: the nation's best educational resources concentrate in the nation's best cities; each province's best resources concentrate in its best city; each city's best resources concentrate in its best school. Three levels of concentration, narrowing level by level — until how high a child's ceiling sits has mostly been decided at the moment of his birth, and his parents' choice of apartment.

First-tier rates: get through that gate, and failing becomes the hard part

Some will say Tsinghua and Peking are too far away — an ordinary first-tier university is enough. The cruel part is that the first-tier line is even more hopeless. These super high schools post first-tier admission rates close to one hundred percent, year after year. Once you are in — and you are not a fool — getting into a first-tier university is nearly automatic; failing to is the difficult outcome.

So the real watershed was never the three days of the gaokao. It is the high-school entrance exam, primary school, the school-district apartment — whether your parents could place you inside that circle before you were old enough to choose anything. The gaokao merely announces, in public, a stratification that was finished long ago.

And in today's economy, the bar for “education changes your fate” keeps rising. A 985 or 211 degree once counted as fate-changing; now perhaps only the Tsinghua–Peking tier reliably cashes that promise, while most 985 and 211 graduates fight for ordinary jobs like everyone else. The threshold rises while the gate narrows — which is exactly why those 350 seats deserve a hard look.

The deeper layer: most doors into Tsinghua and Peking are no longer the gaokao door

If concentrated totals were merely ugly numbers, what comes next is the structural change. In 2026, the High School Affiliated to Nanjing Normal University placed 38 students into Tsinghua and Peking. Guess how many got in on raw gaokao scores alone. Nine.

The other 29 entered through the Strong Foundation Plan, olympiad recommendations, and various special programs. This is not an exception; it is the norm at super high schools, where students admitted on raw scores alone are now the minority.

What does that mean? The rules of competition have changed. Strong Foundation, olympiads, special tracks — these no longer test mainly a student's grinding ability. They test the school's ability: to spot a student's subject talent early enough, to give him professional coaches and advanced courses, to send him into higher-level selections. No student, no single family, can do this alone. It takes real money — hiring Tsinghua and Peking PhDs to teach, buying better laboratory equipment, opening more advanced courses.

So the question becomes: two children with equal talent in mathematics or physics — one born in Haidian and placed in a famous school, one born in a county town and placed in the county high school. Are their chances of being cultivated the same? Certainly not.

Here lies a paradox few people name. Raw-score admission is, in fact, the fairest channel a poor family's child has — it recognizes scores, not resources. Every reform launched under the banner of “breaking score-only admissions” claims to free students, but in practice it moves the contest from “how much can the child endure” to “how much can the school spend, and what does the family know and whom does it know.” One old door closes; a new door opens inside the courtyard of the rich. The talented county kid may never even learn these channels exist.

Mencius's mother moved three times: environment decides almost everything

People like to say a Tsinghua PhD doesn't necessarily teach well, and a good student learns the same anywhere. People who say this have usually never seen what a good environment looks like. Never having seen it, they assume everywhere is the same.

Why did Mencius's mother move three times? Moving is exhausting, housing is expensive. But human beings are products of their environment, and environment decides almost everything. Put a student in the best middle school and his grades can hardly be bad — the school won't allow it. Classmates run ahead, teachers push from behind, resources hang over him like a roof; he cannot even slack off in peace.

More subtly, in that environment a student can actively choose how much energy to spend on exams and what target to aim at: a 985 is enough, a 211 will do — no need to drill like a madman, no need to brainwash himself daily with 600, 650, 700 points. In an ordinary school, students have no such choice; they spend all their strength to buy a far lower ceiling.

Students raised by different schools differ in more than scores. Their thinking differs, their level of understanding differs, and the networks they can reach are worlds apart. None of that is printed on the admission letter, yet it follows a person for life. In the end, where a person stands is very often far more important than how much force he uses.

Conclusion

So the saying “education changes your fate” needs its order corrected: first comes where you stand; only then does education get its chance to change your fate.

Three-level concentration is no longer a story of a few schools being too strong. It is a whole system of resource allocation: the best teachers concentrate in famous schools, the best students concentrate in famous schools, the olympiad and Strong Foundation channels concentrate in famous schools — even the narrative that effort changes fate only still holds inside those walls.

For the hundreds of thousands, the millions of candidates outside the walls, what they lost was never one examination. Most of them never stood on the same starting line to begin with.
